tldr: We achieved autonomous whole-body loco-manipulation with a snake robot, pushing an object to a goal location solely through distributed body contact during sidewinding locomotion without any dedicated arms or grippers.
hero_caption: The snake robot COBRA autonomously transports a box to a goal location using contact pushing with its body flanks. It simultaneously handles propulsion for locomotion and manipulation using whole-body contact.
overview:
Loco-manipulation—simultaneously moving and manipulating—is well known on wheeled or legged robots equipped with arms. On snake robots, however, there is no clear boundary between what counts as a "leg" and what counts as a "hand." Prior research typically attached a gripper to the head or partitioned the body into separate locomotion and manipulation segments. Yet, if we truly leverage a snake's natural flexibility and hyper-redundant body, whole-body loco-manipulation should be possible: propelling forward while pushing an object using the entire body.

This paper tackles this very problem of pushing an object via whole-body contact. Because propulsion and manipulation are tightly coupled, planning trajectories that convey force to an object while gaining ground reaction force for traction becomes extremely complex. To address this, the authors built a contact-implicit dynamic model that unifies robot, ground, and object contacts. Furthermore, to remove the violent periodic oscillations of undulation and simplify planning, they introduced a reduced-order model that treats the entire robot as a bounding box.

In hardware experiments using the 11-joint snake robot COBRA, all 20 pushing trials from varied initial configurations successfully delivered the box to within 0.2 m of the goal location (a 100% success rate). The authors also demonstrated long-distance transport traversing S-shaped waypoints, as well as an optimization simulation that computes physically valid contact forces faster than real time.
contributions: Built an autonomous control system that pushes and transports an object solely through whole-body contact during sidewinding, without relying on dedicated grippers or functional body segmentation.
Proposed a contact-implicit dynamic model that unifies robot, ground, and object interactions within a Moreau–Jean time-stepping scheme.

Developed a reduced-order bounding-box representation that extracts the center of mass and principal inertia axis from the periodic undulatory motion of a snake robot, enabling smooth planning and control.
Achieved a 100% success rate in transporting an object across diverse initial configurations in hardware experiments, and demonstrated complex trajectory tracking across multiple waypoints.

sections.heading: The COBRA Hardware Platform and Task Formulation
sections.summary: This section describes the system configuration of the 11-joint snake robot COBRA and outlines the target task: pushing an object via sidewinding propulsion. Robot and object poses are tracked by a motion capture system, while control calculations run on an onboard Jetson Orin NX in the head module.
sections.details:
### Configuration of the Experimental Robot COBRA
The snake robot "COBRA" used in the experiments consists of 11 articulated joint links alternating between pitch axes (vertical bending) and yaw axes (horizontal bending). Each joint is driven by an independent servomotor connected over an RS-485 communication bus, controlled centrally by a compact Nvidia Jetson Orin NX computer mounted in the head module. The head houses a stereo camera and an IMU (inertial measurement unit), and each joint features an absolute encoder.

### Task Definition
The task addressed in this study is autonomous: given the robot's initial pose and the object's initial position, the robot approaches the target object using sidewinding (a gait where the body undulates diagonally forward like a rattlesnake), pushes it with the flanks of its body, and transports it to a goal location. Current poses of the robot and object are provided by an external motion capture system.

sections.heading: Contact-Implicit Modeling and Oscillation-Free Reduced Representation
sections.summary: The authors propose a contact-implicit model unifying robot, ground, and object contact dynamics, along with a reduced-order model that absorbs periodic undulations to enable smooth trajectory planning. A nominal controller based on geometric Bézier curves stabilizes high-dimensional trajectory optimization computations.
sections.details:
### III-A & III-B Robot and Ground Contact Modeling
Defining the snake robot's head as floating-base coordinates $\bm{q}_{b} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ and joint angles as $\bm{q}_{j} \in \mathbb{R}^{11}$, the Euler–Lagrange equations are partitioned into actuated and unactuated (floating-base) coordinates. Contact dynamics are computed using a Moreau–Jean time-stepping scheme, framing contact impulses between robot–ground and robot–object as a velocity-level complementarity problem. Contact forces satisfying Coulomb friction cones are solved efficiently at each step via a Projected Gauss–Seidel (PGS) algorithm.

### III-C Robot–Object–Ground Interactions
The pushed object (box) is modeled as a 3-DOF planar rigid body in the horizontal plane. Contact forces from the robot act as an external wrench on the box's side, while ground interactions are approximated by two contact points placed in front of and behind the center of mass. Ground contact forces are solved algebraically and rapidly without iterative calculations, using the box's acceleration conditions and projection onto friction polyhedra.

### III-D Reduced-Order Representation Smoothing Periodic Undulations
When a snake robot sidewinds, its head and individual links constantly experience severe oscillations. Using these raw motions as trajectory tracking targets causes control to fail. To resolve this, the authors compute the center of mass $\bm{p}_{bb}$ from all link mass positions, and extract the principal inertia axis via singular value decomposition (SVD) to define the overall robot heading $\theta_{bb}$. This lets the planner treat the entire robot as a single smoothly moving "bounding box" with 3 degrees of freedom.

### III-E & III-F Gait Generation and Nominal Controller
The 11 joint trajectories are driven by sinusoidal central pattern generators (CPGs), steering the angular velocity by shifting an asymmetric amplitude bias $\Delta$ on the yaw joints. A high-level planner smoothly switches between an approach phase (quadratic Bézier curve) and a pushing phase (cubic Bézier curve), using a pure-pursuit law and proportional controller to determine $\Delta$. This feedforward input serves as a strong warm-start initialization for contact-implicit trajectory optimization.

captions.F2: Comparison between the full-order model (left) and the reduced-order model (right). By reducing the periodic undulatory motion of each link into a 3-DOF bounding-box pose $\bm{q}_{bb}$, the system enables smooth trajectory planning from approach to pushing without being disrupted by oscillations.
captions.F4: Reference trajectory generation using Bézier curves. A smooth path is created using a quadratic Bézier curve during the object approach phase (left), and a cubic Bézier curve accounting for the relative robot–object geometry during the loco-manipulation pushing phase to the goal (right).

sections.heading: Hardware Experiments: 100% Success Rate and Waypoint Tracking
sections.summary: Using the physical COBRA robot, 20 transport trials from varying initial positions achieved a 100% success rate. The robot also completed a long-distance, sharp-turning task traversing two intermediate waypoints, and simplified trajectory optimization simulations confirmed that physically consistent contact forces can be computed faster than real time.
sections.details:
### Hardware Experimental Setup
Experiments used a sidewinding gait with pitch amplitude $\alpha_p = 15^\circ$, yaw amplitude $\alpha_y = 40^\circ$, frequency $\omega = 0.5\text{ Hz}$, and an average forward speed of roughly $0.1\text{ m/s}$. The steering bias $\Delta$ was constrained to $[-15^\circ, +15^\circ]$ running at a control rate of $0.75\text{ Hz}$. The transported object was a rectangular box of mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ and dimensions $0.2 \times 0.12\text{ m}$.

### Pushing Results and Stability
Across 20 hardware trials with varied starting and goal positions for the robot and object, the system achieved a 100% success rate in bringing the box to within $0.2\text{ m}$ of the goal location. While turning during the approach induced small lateral offsets between the box and robot, feedback control compensated for these shifts and stably delivered the box into the goal area.

### Continuous Transport Across Multiple Waypoints
In a long-distance trial sequentially visiting two waypoints (WP1, WP2) before reaching the goal, the robot executed sharp turns exceeding $200^\circ$ while maintaining continuous contact. Although transient heading error spikes occurred at waypoint transitions, they quickly converged back to near zero.

### Optimization Model Validity and Computational Speed
A single-shooting optimization (horizon $1.25\text{ s}$, time step $\Delta t = 0.025\text{ s}$) was solved using contact force $\bm{F}$ and contact location $c_x$ as decision variables to reconstruct the box's recorded motion trajectory. The resulting robot–box contact forces stayed consistently within the pushing direction of the friction cone, while ground friction forces sat exactly on the boundary of the friction polyhedron, matching continuous kinetic sliding friction. Optimizing the entire ~145-second trajectory finished in under one minute, confirming better-than-real-time computation speeds.

captions.F5: Hardware loco-manipulation experimental results. Top: snapshots and XY-plane trajectories for a representative trial. Bottom: four trials across varied configurations. In all setups, the reduced-order model tracks smoothly and pushes the box to the goal.
captions.F7: Continuous transport experiment traversing two waypoints (WP1, WP2) (top) and the contact optimization simulation based on that trajectory (bottom). Contact is maintained even through sharp turns, and the pushing and friction forces computed in simulation remain properly within friction limits.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: This study demonstrated, both experimentally and in simulation, that autonomous whole-body loco-manipulation via distributed snake robot contacts is viable. Future directions point toward adapting to uneven terrain and achieving full autonomy using only onboard sensors without external motion capture.
sections.details:
### Paper Conclusions
By combining a Moreau–Jean time-stepping contact-implicit dynamic model with a reduced-order bounding-box representation that smooths periodic oscillations, the authors proved that precise and stable whole-body loco-manipulation is possible even with a gripperless snake robot. Because the nominal controller provides high-quality initial solutions, this work charts a path toward solving optimization problems without predefined contact schedules at near real-time speeds.

### Future Challenges and Directions
For immediate extensions, the authors cite implementing a full-order contact-implicit trajectory optimization loop on hardware that includes full snake dynamics, allowing adaptive gait adjustments on rough terrain beyond flat ground. Furthermore, they aim to replace external motion capture tracking with onboard visual-inertial odometry and object detection using the head-mounted stereo camera and IMU, targeting autonomous deployment in unstructured real-world environments.

takeaways: Even without dedicated arms or grippers, snake robots can perform highly practical non-prehensile pushing manipulation using whole-body flank contacts during sidewinding.
For robots with periodic undulatory gaits, using a "reduced-order bounding box" derived from the center of mass and SVD principal inertia axis as the planning space dramatically stabilizes control.

A contact-implicit formulation eliminates the need to pre-specify contact timings or locations, enabling unified analysis and optimization of multi-point contact where locomotion and manipulation merge into one.
limitations: Current hardware experiments are restricted to flat, uniform rigid ground, leaving whole-body loco-manipulation unverified on uneven terrains such as sand or stepped surfaces.
Robot and object pose tracking currently depends on an overhead motion capture system, falling short of standalone full autonomy using onboard cameras and IMUs.
Overall optimization including full-order robot dynamics is currently simplified even in simulation, and has not yet been executed as a closed-loop online replanning system on physical hardware.
